## Observations
1. Since all three integers are at least 1, the product of two of them is at least as large as either factor. Thus, in any valid arrangement, the product is a largest input value.
2. Sorting the three values gives \(x \le y \le z\), so the only equality to check is \(x \times y = z\). Ties do not change this check, because swapping equal values leaves the factors and product unchanged.
3. The input always contains exactly three integers, so sorting them and checking one product takes constant time and space.

## Solution sketch
1. “Since all three integers are at least 1, the product of two of them is at least as large as either factor. Thus, in any valid arrangement, the product is a largest input value.”  
   Read the three integers and sort them in nondecreasing order so that the last value is the candidate product.
2. “Sorting the three values gives \(x \le y \le z\), so the only equality to check is \(x \times y = z\). Ties do not change this check, because swapping equal values leaves the factors and product unchanged.”  
   Multiply the first two values. If the result equals the last value, print `Yes`; otherwise, print `No`. No special handling is needed for repeated values or for 1: for example, \(1, k, k\) passes the same check.
3. “The input always contains exactly three integers, so sorting them and checking one product takes constant time and space.”  
   The algorithm uses \(O(1)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space.
